Features include multimedia learning technologies, web-enhanced learning systems, and ergonomic furnishings. Students assigned to the classroom reported that they felt much closer to faculty. The Takeaway: It's not just about the teaching but about the classroom environment too.

Having been forced in the past to compete against each other to raise enrollment and increase funding, eight institutions in southern West Virginia recently joined together to form a higher education center. The participants are Bluefield State College, West Virginia University Institute of Technology, Concord University, Marshall University, the WVU Extension Service, New River Community and Technical College, Southern West Virginia Community and Technical College, and WVU Tech.

The Takeaway: Sharing facilities, instructors, and students can drive down costs and increase students' access to higher education.

The University of New Hampshire, which operates the state's largest public transit system, has three regional and seven campus transit routes. Faculty, staff, students, and Durham residents ride free. At West Virginia University, Personal Rapid Transit is a computer-operated system that provides transportation for the campus and community over an 8.2-mile track. Students, whose undergraduate tuition fees finance the system, simply swipe their IDs to get on board. And then there is the Mocs Express at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, which makes 24 stops along a circular route around the campus perimeter. Nearly 87,000 students rode the Mocs Express in 2006.

The Takeaway: Promoting alternative methods of transportation not only helps combat pollution but also makes campuses safer and creates a more collegial atmosphere as pedestrian traffic increases.

Design build contractors are generally familiar with the risk they are assuming under the traditional design-build model in which the contractor is responsible for the design, as well as the construction of the design his team has created. However, contractors are less familiar with the risks that are assumed under a design-bid-build model in which there are some elements of design delegation.

Typically, under the design-bid-build model, the owner assumed all responsibilities for the design and might even have impliedly warranted the sufficiency of that design under the Spearin Doctrine or otherwise. Under this scenario, the contractor could rely on the plans and specifications that were provided to him and if he constructed them in accordance with the plans and specifications, he would have an absolute defense should there be a problem later. However, in recent years there has been some shifting of that risk where more design delegation is being transferred from the Owner and design professional to the contractor by agreement.

For example, AIA documents now include a design delegation clause in A201, section 3.12.10. Under that section, if specified by the contract documents, the contractor is responsible for the specified design components including providing proof through a designer’s seal that the design satisfies the performance and/or design criteria provided in the contract documents, and the Owner and its designer can rely upon that delegated design.

In addition, there are many design elements, whether it would be shoring, connections, or loads that are traditionally handled by the contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers performing the work. Architects are increasingly using the contract documents

The Name of the Game in Design-Build Contracts? Document, Document, Document!

Michael McKenna and Timothy Ryan | Cohen Seglias Pallas Greenhall & Furman

Design-build contracts (and their lesser utilized counterpart—engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contracts) are prevalent in the construction industry. Though far from a new contractual relationship, design-build contracts are increasingly chosen by owners in an attempt to reduce risks and costs. The design-build model differs from the “traditional” design-bid-build model in that, with the traditional model, an owner is often very involved in both the initial design of the project and design decisions during the course of construction. An owner is given the opportunity during the design-bid-build process to tweak the design so that it truly becomes what they want. Design issues based on incorrect original assumptions can be worked out with revisions to the design prior to putting it out to bid. Further, in the traditional model, a design professional is generally retained by an owner and serves as the owner’s representative throughout the duration of a project.

In a design-build contract, on the other hand, the process is “streamlined.” At some point, the contractor becomes responsible for both the design and construction of a project. There is no doubt that the owner buys themselves a single point of contact. However, in exchange for that single point of contact and “fixed” price, the owner forgoes the ongoing customization options available in the traditional model. The Many Paths (and Perils) of Construction Projects: What you don’t know can hurt you, what you do know can save time and money

While some companies routinely engage in construction projects, for other companies a construction project can be a once in a decade experience. Some companies have experienced in-house personnel to guide them through a building project while others need to rely upon third-party professionals to evaluate the company’s needs and direct the project. No matter where your company falls within the spectrum of experience, knowing what your options are, what questions to ask along the way, and how to properly address the legal risks will save your company time and money as well as help it to avoid costly claims.

Project Delivery Methods

The first step in a significant construction project is to determine the most cost-effective manner of having your project designed and built. From the inception there are two primary options available to an owner. Deciding what option best suits your company’s needs in advance of consulting with third parties ensures that your company’s needs are met while at the same time, the company is not taking on more risk than is required.

In the traditional design-bid-build model, the owner (you) engages an architect or engineer and works with them to evaluate the company’s needs and to design the building. Once the design is complete, the project can be competitively bid based on a complete set of plans and specifications, and the owner has the option to award the project to the lowest responsible bidder. A private owner can also evaluate the competitive prices and engage the contractor of its choosing at a negotiated price. In this model, the owner has two contracts to administer – one with the design professional and one with the contractor. When using this approach, it is important to ensure that the two contracts are consistent as to responsibilities and dispute resolution forums. This avoids (where a dispute arises) a scenario in which an owner is litigating with the design professional in court and at the same time defending a claim by the contractor in an arbitration tribunal or vice versa. Compounding the complexity is that typical arbitration provisions do not allow for the joinder of additional parties. While courts permit joinder of parties, a party may raise an arbitration clause as an affirmative defense to its joinder, thereby splitting the case in two actions. As a result, the owner may incur double the legal fees and risk inconsistent results.

Architects | Design & Build

In the fast-paced construction industry, the design-build model is rapidly gaining popularity across the UK. This innovative approach combines architectural design and construction services into one streamlined process. As a result, it offers an efficient way to execute complex projects. More architects and builders are adopting this method, which is transforming the landscape of UK architecture and construction.

What is Design-Build Architecture?

Design-build is a project delivery method where a single entity, usually a firm or partnership, manages both the design and construction phases. This approach differs from the traditional design-bid-build model, where design and construction are handled separately. In the design-build model, architects and builders collaborate from the very beginning. This ensures a unified vision and smooth execution throughout the project.

Why is Design-Build Gaining Popularity?

Efficiency and Speed:
One of the key benefits of the design-build approach is its efficiency. With a single point of contact, communication is more straightforward, allowing decisions to be made faster. Consequently, this often results in shorter project timelines. The overlap between design and construction phases reduces delays and speeds up project delivery.

Cost-Effectiveness:
Design-build projects typically have more predictable budgets. Since design and construction teams work together from the start, they can identify potential issues early on. This minimizes the risk of expensive changes later in the project. Moreover, this integrated approach enables better cost control and value engineering, adjusting the design to meet the budget without compromising on quality.

Enhanced Collaboration:
The design-build model fosters a collaborative environment. Architects and builders function as a cohesive team, which leads to better communication and fewer conflicts. This shared commitment to the project’s success also encourages innovative solutions. The design and construction teams can brainstorm together, bringing creative ideas to life.

Key Differences Between Design-Build Firms and Construction Contractors

  1. Responsibility and Management: The most significant difference between a design-build firm and a construction contractor is the level of responsibility. In a design-build model, one firm handles both design and construction, streamlining communication and decision-making. In contrast, a construction contractor manages only the construction phase, following the plans laid out by a separate design team.
  2. Project Timeline: Design-build firms tend to accelerate project timelines because they integrate design and construction phases. Construction contractors, on the other hand, follow a more traditional sequential model where design must be fully completed before construction begins.
  3. Cost Control: Design-build firms often offer better cost control, as they work within a budget from the beginning and can make real-time adjustments during the design phase to avoid exceeding financial limits. With construction contractors, there can be cost overruns if design flaws or unexpected construction challenges arise.
  4. Collaboration and Innovation: In a design-build model, collaboration is fostered from the start, allowing for creative and practical solutions that benefit the project. In the traditional design-bid-build model, there is often less opportunity for innovation, as the design is completed before the contractor is brought in.

The choice between a design-build firm and a construction contractor depends on the specific needs and goals of your project. Design-build firms offer streamlined management, faster timelines, and enhanced collaboration by handling both design and construction. On the other hand, construction contractors provide specialized expertise during the construction phase and allow clients flexibility in selecting separate designers and builders. Evaluating the scope, complexity, and budget of your project will help determine which approach is best suited for achieving a successful outcome.

In this article, we explain what construction technology is, how it benefits the construction sector, the safety and training requirements for the best results and the types of technology set to affect the construction sector.

What is construction technology?

The term construction technology describes innovative tools used during the development phase of construction projects. Construction tools have some level of automation and improve construction methods. Some people include tech tools used during the design phase in this definition, while others designate them as preconstruction technology.

Related: 5 Technological Skills for Professionals (With Benefits)

Benefits of construction technologies

Here are some of the benefits of construction technologies:

Improve site productivity

Construction technologies help teams plan and execute their duties better, which improves productivity. Modern models and simulation tools are important planning tools that help construction teams see structures before commencing construction, so they can build them right the first time and reduce resource waste. Power tools are also much more efficient than hand tools. A carpenter can cut wood much quicker using a power saw than a hand saw, for example. Off-site construction is another technological advancement boosting productivity on large-scale projects. New construction technologies aim to make construction more productive by streamlining processes more than the traditional design-bid-build model.

Related: How to Measure Productivity in the Workplace: Complete Guide

Make stronger structures

Construction technology can make projects stronger by helping teams design and build better structures. Construction software makes collaborating on construction projects easier, ensuring a range of professionals can pool their ideas to create better designs. Construction teams can also use simulations and models to test their structures and redesign them to be more durable. Technological tools for preparing sites and constructing structures also allow teams to make stronger structures than they could by hand.

Allow for taller structures

Technological tools including cranes and forklifts elevate construction workers more than ladders, allowing them to work at much greater heights. With the use of cordless power tools, they can create taller structures than construction workers of the past. Building taller structures has become vital for creating new structures in densely populated cities with limited vacant land.

Can improve site safety

A move toward digital documentation makes circulating important information, such as maintenance reports and safety procedures easier. Smart tools and drones can monitor employees and their environments, allowing supervisors to keep their employees safe more effectively than ever before. Training that incorporates technology can more effectively prepare construction workers for challenging duties.
